record.paper_title: Regularity of maximal operators: recent progress and some open problems
record.original_question: Let M be the one-dimensional centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Is the derivative map f -> (M f)' continuous from W^{1,1}(R) to L^1(R)? Equivalently, whenever f_j converges to f in W^{1,1}(R), must (M f_j)' converge to (M f)' in L^1(R)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a locally integrable function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, define the (one-dimensional) centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function by
$$ (Mf)(x) \;=\; \sup_{r>0} \frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r} |f(y)|\,dy. $$
Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Sobolev space of functions $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ whose distributional derivative $f'$ belongs to $L^1(\mathbb{R})$, equipped with the norm $\|f\|_{W^{1,1}} = \|f\|_{L^1} + \|f'\|_{L^1}$. It is known that if $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ then $Mf$ is weakly differentiable and $(Mf)'\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, so that the map $T: f \mapsto (Mf)'$ is well-defined from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ to $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

Determine whether $T$ is continuous: that is, if $f_j \to f$ in $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$, must $(Mf_j)' \to (Mf)'$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$?
artifact.status_search_result: A 2023 paper "Continuity for the one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator at the derivative level" (arXiv:2109.09691, published in J. Funct. Anal.) establishes that the map f ↦ (Mf)' is continuous from W^{1,1}(ℝ) to L^1(ℝ), thereby answering this question affirmatively.
